rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods, Field Experiments <U+2013> two-season field experiment (2017, 2018) on a calcareous sandy soil at Sohag, Egypt, split-plot design with four replications testing P fertigation frequency and P form on potato; own yield, petiole P, soil pH and available P data (Tables 4-6, Figs 1-2).
rows.notes: The study is a primary field trial, but every treatment (including the control) was drip-irrigated with the same daily water amount; the factors varied were P fertigation frequency (daily, 2-day, 3-day) and P fertiliser form (urea phosphate vs monopotassium phosphate). There is no comparison of drip with any other irrigation method, and no measurement of water distribution uniformity, waterlogging, dry patches or plant stress. What the study shows is that daily fertigation of urea phosphate under drip increased petiole P, marketable/total tuber yield, PUE and WUE relative to less frequent fertigation and MPP (e.g. ~10% marketable yield gain for daily vs other frequencies; ~22% for daily UP vs MPP every 3 days). This is evidence about fertigation management, not about drip irrigation delivering uniform water supply or higher productivity versus other systems.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods, Field Experiments <U+2013> own two-season (2017, 2018) field experiment on drip-irrigated potato on a calcareous sandy soil in Sohag, Egypt, with yield, petiole P, soil pH and available P measured (Tables 4-6, Figs 1-2).
rows.notes: No result on risk reduction (plant stress, waterlogging, dry patches, yield-reduction risk) attributable to drip irrigation. All plots were drip-irrigated identically; the experiment varied only P fertigation frequency and P form. The study reports higher yields, PUE and WUE for daily urea-phosphate fertigation versus less frequent fertigation and monopotassium phosphate, which concerns fertiliser management under drip rather than drip irrigation's effect on water distribution uniformity or stress risk relative to other irrigation methods.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study tests P fertigation frequency and P fertiliser form under a uniform drip irrigation regime on potato in sandy calcareous soil; it contains no drip-versus-other-method comparison and no measurement of water distribution uniformity, waterlogging or plant stress, so it cannot support the cited passage about drip irrigation per se.
